title: Homily on the Forefeast of the Dormition

pairs.en: Yesterday, following the direction of the Holy Church, we came down from Tabor, lit by the last rays of light from the face of the transfigured Lord. Today, following the same guidance of the Church, we must pass over to Gethsemane — to the tomb of the Mother of God, to behold “the final mystery accomplished in her.” Tabor is radiant with divine joy; but Gethsemane, too, is sweet to the soul. There the face of the Son shines with the unfading light of the Godhead; here the tomb of the Mother becomes a ladder to heaven. There Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak of His departure, so that by their very presence they might point out, in the person of Jesus, the One who is Lord not of the living only, but of the dead as well; here Gabriel, the minister of wonders, appears with a branch from paradise, to bring the earthborn the good news that she who descends into the tomb is more honourable than the Cherubim and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim. There the Godhead shines before the disciples from behind the veil of the flesh, so that “when they see Him crucified, they may understand that His suffering was voluntary”; here, on the eve of the heavenly glory of the Ever-Virgin, the weakness of her humanity is laid open, so that when we see her at the right hand of the throne of her Son and God, we may know that this greatness is the work not of the Mother's nature, but of the Son's grace.

In Gethsemane the human weakness of the Son was destined to show itself in its fullest measure: there He was drenched in a sweat of blood; there He was strengthened by an angel. And in Gethsemane, too, the human weaknesses of the Mother were destined to appear for the last time: here her eyes, her lips, and her hands were closed; here her most holy soul was released, though only for a short time, from her most pure body.

After this, do we need to look for any other subject for our instruction today than this: that all of us carry our thoughts to the deathbed of the Most Blessed one, at which all the apostles but one are now gathered? Let us briefly repeat in words what they saw with their eyes.

After the Lord's ascension into heaven, and after the descent of the Spirit, the Comforter, upon the apostles in the form of tongues of fire, the dwelling place of the Mother of God for a time was not Jerusalem, but the city from which Saint John came and where he lived — John, to whom she had been entrusted from the Cross in place of a mother. *From that hour,* we read in the Gospel, *that disciple took her unto his own home* (John 19:27).

However peaceful that refuge was, and however tender and holy the care that surrounded her in the house of Jesus' beloved disciple, her mother's heart drew her back to Jerusalem — to the place where almost every path was marked by the footsteps of her Son and God, and where every spot brought to mind either His glory or His suffering. After her return to that city, her favourite occupation, as tradition tells us, was to walk in the precious footprints of her beloved Son: to pray where He had prayed, to rest where He had rested. Golgotha, the Mount of Olives, and Gethsemane therefore enjoyed the sight of the Grace-filled one more often than other places. Gethsemane, indeed, became at last her constant final refuge on earth. Following the example of her Son, who three times had prayed here to the point of a bloody sweat, she spent whole days and nights in prayer in the midst of the olive garden. What did she pray for? She prayed, no doubt, for the swift spread of saving faith in her Son across the whole face of the earth; she prayed for the conversion to faith and to the knowledge of the truth of the Jewish people, perishing in unbelief and hardness of heart; she prayed for the new Churches which the apostles were planting in various lands and among various peoples; she prayed, no doubt, for all the future Churches as well, which were to be planted by their disciples and successors — and so she prayed also for us, who in our own time were counted worthy to be enlightened by the light of the Gospel faith. But all her prayers ended with one petition: that she might soon be released from the bonds of the flesh, so as to see for ever, face to face, the One who, after His ascension into heaven, as a sign of the impassibility of His Godhead, no longer appeared to her.

sections.heading: A prayer long unanswered — and why

pairs.en: Could a prayer so pure and holy, one would think, fail to be heard soon and granted at once? Yet it was not soon — not soon at all — that it was heard and granted. From this let us learn, by the example of the Mother of God, not to grow weary in our own supplications, and not to take it as a sign of inattention from above when something happens to us that runs contrary to our pleas and desires. For the Ever-Virgin herself, of course, it would have been better to pass sooner to her Son in heaven and, in place of the bonds of the flesh, to begin to enjoy the majesty above the heavens. But for the consolation of Christ's apostles — so that, deprived of the visible presence of their Teacher and Lord, they might find a common refuge with His most holy Mother according to the flesh — the Most Blessed Virgin had to remain on earth; and she remained no small time: more than two decades.

But at last the long-desired hour of her departure drew near. Forty days before her death, in the midst of her fervent prayers to her Son that it might be hastened, the Mother of God beheld before her the Archangel — the very one who had once announced to her the joy of her conceiving without knowing man. Foretelling the time of her departure, the heavenly messenger handed her, on behalf of her Son and God, a branch from paradise, to stand at her tomb as a sign of victory over death.

sections.heading: The apostles gather; the Virgin falls asleep

pairs.en: For her who had long lived in spirit and heart with her Son in heaven, no desire remained on earth except one: to see the apostles once more at her bedside before her death, to be comforted by their faith and love, to speak over them a last blessing of the Mother of God, and to hearten and inspire them with the hope of her intercession at the throne of her Son. But to achieve this by ordinary means was utterly impossible, for the apostles had long since scattered to preach across the whole face of the earth. Only the power of God could accomplish it directly — and that power was not slow to act. Borne, as tradition says, upon the clouds, all the apostles except Thomas streamed together to Gethsemane for the day of the Ever-Virgin's Dormition. Surrounded by this holy company, comforted by their love, in the midst of her prayer and theirs, the Mother of God gave up her spirit in peace into the hands of her Son and God.

When the most pure body had been committed to the earth and laid within the cave of Gethsemane, on the third day Saint Thomas also arrived. God so arranged it, that the same apostle whose unbelief in the Son's resurrection had served to make His Godhead manifest should also become the instrument for revealing the glory of His Mother. Deprived of the consolation of seeing the Mother of God still living, Saint Thomas begged his fellow apostles to grant him the mercy of at least beholding her lifeless body, to be sanctified by kissing it and venerating it as the ark of holiness and the dwelling place of the glory of the Lord. But when the apostles, wishing to satisfy this pure desire, opened the tomb in the cave, it proved to be entirely empty. The holy body had been translated to where her glorified soul already was, so that, like the Son, the Mother too should not see corruption in her body. Then all understood that Thomas's very delay had been the work not of chance but of the Providence of God, so that through it the translation of the Mother of God, body and all, into heaven might be revealed to the whole world.

sections.heading: Wondrous her entry into the world, wondrous her departure

pairs.en: Such is the holy account of the Dormition of the Mother of God, as it has been handed down to us by the ancient God-bearing fathers. Wondrous was her entry into this world; wondrous, too, her departure from it! She who carried in her womb and in her arms the One who carries all things could not, like ordinary daughters of men, become food for the grave. The debt to nature was paid: as one born of earth, she died in the flesh. But grace also showed itself in all its power: as the Mother of Life, she visibly ascended, by way of the tomb, to life and glory.

Let us stand in reverence before these mysteries and wonders! Let us bless and glorify her who ascended into heaven with her body for this very purpose — to be a protection and intercession for the whole world. But at the same time, let us not go away from her tomb empty — without spiritual instruction. The Saviour did not say in vain that those who faithfully do the will of His Father are as His mother and His brethren. This means that if we, like the Mother of God, walk blamelessly in the law of the Lord, then, like her, we too shall become partakers of the Lord's grace, given without stint. That grace, feeding, strengthening, illumining, and sanctifying us throughout our life, cannot fail to show itself also in the hour of our death. How? Not, of course, by the translation of our frail flesh into heaven (what would it do there, with its impurity?), but by making our end such as the Church in her prayers desires for us all — without shame, peaceful, and free of pain. For us, so far from perfect, this gift alone is enough — if only the Lord would be pleased to grant it to each one of us! Amen.
